items.title: David N. Baker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: But the people who were my friends – Buell Neidlinger, Charlie Haden, and all those guys – were all people who were thought of as a part of the avant garde.

ctx.x: Can you put your activities in the avant garde in a time frame? When we lived with Charles in New York, that was ’78, ’79, but I know you’re talking about activities from a somewhat earlier time.

It varied, because when we were with George Russell – once I was a convert, once I got past feeling threatened by Ornette – what we played belonged in that category. And a lot of the music that I played in Indianapolis when I moved back there and was switching to cello, had to be called pretty much avant-garde music. This was music that I was playing with Willis Kirk, I was playing with Chuck [Carter]. We went through a period for one year, when I had a group with David Lahm, that we played only the music of…

retro – if you stop and think of the use of movie music and stuff, it’s very romantic and very beautiful. But then [at that time] and then again in the time that I was around with Charles Tyler, was back into the avant garde. And actually my first years here at Indiana University, it was packed. You couldn’t get in a concert, whenever we played. And what we were playing was really out. I would have orchestras with people positioned all around the room, playing.
